Article Title: Colorado had more than 80,000 lesser prairie-chickens in 1975 but counted only 89 breeding males in 2024; a land trust has now spent nearly $2 million on a 2,100-acre ranch to help bring them back
Article Text:
The birds live in the Sand Sagebrush Ecoregion, which stretches across southeastern Colorado, southwestern Kansas and a small part of western Oklahoma. (American Bird Conservancy photo)

Habitat loss has reduced the population

CPW has used translocation to help the birds

Federal protection changed in 2026

Colorado’s lesser prairie-chicken population has fallen from more than 80,000 birds in 1975 to just 89 breeding males, according to a 2024 data. To restore the population of the critically threatened grassland bird, nearly 2,100 acres of land in the state’s southeastern plains have now been acquired.The Southern Plains Land Trust bought the former private ranch in August for just under $2 million through grants and donations, Rocky Mountain PBS reported. The property is in Kiowa County and lies next to the Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site.The land trust will work with Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) to restore the property. Work is expected to begin next winter or spring, with the aim of allowing the grassland to recover and restoring key plant species needed by lesser prairie-chickens.The location of the new preserve is within 10 miles of an active lesser prairie-chicken “lek”. A lek is a traditional breeding ground where male birds gather during mating season to display and compete for mates.Henry Pollock, an ecologist, conservation biologist and executive director of the Southern Plains Land Trust, said habitat loss and overgrazing have played a major role in the species’ decline.“The lesser prairie-chickens are declining rapidly. A lot of that is due to habitat loss and also overgrazing on remaining grassland,” Pollock said.“By letting the land rest and recover a little bit and restoring some of these key grass species for breeding, we hope that they will recolonise naturally, although there is the possibility that we could do a translocation in the future,” he added.Lesser prairie-chickens are brown and white grassland birds about the size of a soccer ball. They weigh between one and two pounds. During mating season, males inflate air sacs in their necks, making their reddish or orange patches more noticeable to females.The birds live in the Sand Sagebrush Ecoregion, which stretches across southeastern Colorado, southwestern Kansas and a small part of western Oklahoma. CPW lists habitat loss and fragmentation, energy development, agriculture and grazing, and climate change among the threats to the species.Habitat loss has also left the birds living in scattered areas. Pollock said some breeding habitat has been grazed away, including the grasses and smaller habitats used by the birds for nesting.“The lesser prairie-chickens, over a long period of time, some of their breeding habitat has kind of been grazed off the landscape. That includes bunch grasses and little micro habitats for where they have their nest,” Pollock said.The new property is expected to provide an area where grassland can recover and habitat can be restored close to an existing breeding site.CPW hasalso carried out translocation projects, moving lesser prairie-chickens from one area to another. From 2016 through 2019, CPW worked with Kansas to move 411 birds from the Short-Grass Prairie in northwestern Kansas to the Sand Sagebrush Ecoregion. The birds were released at the Comanche National Grasslands in Colorado and the Cimarron National Grasslands in southwestern Kansas.The project produced early signs of success. One year after it ended, the relocated birds had established 20 leks across the two sites. There were 115 males and an estimated population of about 250 birds in total, according to wildlife biologist Jonathan Reitz, who worked on the project.“At the end of the day, that’s really successful. If somebody told me at the front end that for every two birds that you move, one is actually going to get established in a population, I would have been ecstatic because these birds are getting moved to an entirely different landscape,” Reitz said.However, the population later declined. Reitz said years of drought in the region contributed to the decline.The project also showed the importance of suitable habitat for the birds after they are moved. Reitz said land needs to be managed properly if conservation efforts are to improve conditions for the species.“The situation is really dire. You need land that’s going to be managed properly for the chicken,” Reitz said. “And the reality is if we want those lands managed in a way that’s going to improve things for some of the wildlife species, we’ve got to figure out ways to pay for it.”The new preserve comes as the lesser prairie-chicken’s federal protection has changed. The US Fish and Wildlife Service removed both the northern and southern distinct population segments from the federal Endangered Species Act list in 2026 in response to a court order.The southern population had been listed as endangered and the northern population as threatened in 2022. Despite the removal, Pollock said the species remains the most endangered bird in the Southern Great Plains.
Article Summary: Colorado’s lesser prairie-chicken population has fallen from more than 80,000 birds in 1975 to just 89 breeding males. The birds live in the Sand Sagebrush Ecoregion, which stretches across southeastern Colorado, southwestern Kansas and a small part of western Oklahoma. The Southern Plains Land Trust bought the former private ranch in August for just under $2 million.

Article Title: ​A New Jersey family bought Atlantic City's historic Steel Pier for $4.25 million in 2011; 15 years later, the 5.2-acre amusement landmark is asking $85 million, with possibilities to redevelop it
Article Text:
A long history

The Long Kiss Goodnight

The Bounty Hunter

Cake Boss

The Catanoso family bought it for $4.25 million

What’s next for Steel Pier?

Atlantic City’s iconic Steel Pier is up for sale, offering a rare chance to buy an operating amusement park built over the Atlantic Ocean, along with the rights to extend the property much farther into the sea. The asking price is $85 million, according to a report by the New York Post.The nearly 1,000-foot-long pier sits directly across the boardwalk from the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino and covers roughly 5.2 acres. Ryan Serhant, Michele Zyska and Kevin Bergin of Serhant have listed the property.A piece of New Jersey history, the pier has survived a Depression, two world wars, organised crime, urban decay and a 1969 fire that burned away nearly a third of its original footprint. It remains a classic Jersey Shore amusement park, with a towering Ferris wheel, rides, games and food, along with a built-in helipad. Now it awaits a new buyer.Steel Pier has been part of Atlantic City’s identity for more than a century. It was constructed in 1897 and started operation a year later as a theatre. Once known as the ‘Showplace of the Nation’, it stretched nearly 2,300 feet at its height. It hosted performances from Frank Sinatra to the radio stars of the 1940s.A young Tony Grant launched his ‘Stars of Tomorrow’ talent showcase there, later creating the groundwork for what would become American Bandstand. The pier also appeared in films such as ‘’ and ‘’ and the TV show ‘’. For a brief period in the 1930s, Steel Pier was also the official venue of the Miss America contest.The current structure was rebuilt using steel-reinforced concrete in the late 1980s. It is anchored roughly 90 feet into bedrock and, according to the listing materials, remained intact during Superstorm Sandy in 2012.Now, the pier remains an amusement park, attracting thousands of visitors with its rides, games and the Ferris wheel overlooking the Atlantic.The Steel Pier was run by longtime South Jersey amusement operators for nearly two decades before the Catanoso family, including brothers Anthony, Charles and William Catanoso, purchased it. When the Catanoso brothers took over Atlantic City's Steel Pier fourteen years ago, they inherited more than carnival rides and a 965-foot boardwalk landmark. They inherited history. In 2011, they bought the property for $4.25 million. Now, the asking price is $85 million, twenty times what they paid for!The jump from $4.25 million to $85 million isn’t simply because of inflation or market cycles. It reflects how the property is valued now. What the Catanoso family operated as a working amusement park, a summer attraction with the Ferris wheel, games, food and the helipad on the roof, it repositioned as something far more valuable. Steel Pier is currently about 150 feet wide and 965 feet long. A perpetual riparian grant allows the property to extend as far as 2,850 feet into the Atlantic Ocean. The existing pier footprint could also potentially be expanded by 25%, according to listing materials. According to Serhant, this is the opportunity to own a piece of ocean. “How often does someone get to own a piece of the ocean? That’s exactly what this offers,” Serhant said in a statement.“The Steel Pier isn’t just 5 acres on the most famous boardwalk in the world, it actually offers the chance to own the Atlantic itself and build something unforgettable on top of it,” he added.In 2008, Steel Pier was approved and permitted for a condo-hotel entertainment complex. So the possibilities are huge. According to Serhant, it is a “developable American history that extends straight into the Atlantic Ocean.”This sale will also bring an end to the Catanoso family’s association with the historic landmark. “The next generation is pursuing other passions. So rather than keep it in the family, they’d rather see it go to an owner who can really realise its full potential,” Zyska told The Post.The property was valued at $87 million last year, after substantial improvements. But according to Serhant, the current asking price is indeed a steal. “If this were in Palm Beach, it would be $400 million, and someone would have bought it already. The fact that it’s even available and there’s an opportunity to purchase it, I just think is super, super special,” Serhant said.The new owner would not necessarily have to keep it as an amusement park. It can be anything. A luxury hotel-residence with retail and entertainment, a music venue or experiential complex, or a residential tower with a commercial base is also possible with 2,850 feet of ocean development rights that no competitor on the boardwalk can match. The 40,000 sq. ft. front building and sky bridge carry an easement into the neighbouring Hard Rock’s convention floor, but the existing pier footprint could potentially be expanded by 25%.Serhant has already conducted what he calls ‘soft conversations with a handful’ of potential buyers. “Executing on a condo-hotel plan would probably be my first plan. You have the rare ability to build out over the ocean itself,” he told the outlet.“If you’re a high-end, high-net-worth hospitality builder, I think Atlantic City is incredible value,” Serhant added.Zyska sees the possibility of music and entertainment uses given the prime location. “If it lands in the right hands, it can really transform the boardwalk, and even that stretch of the Atlantic. It’s really a premier opportunity,” she said.
Article Summary: The nearly 1,000-foot-long pier sits directly across the boardwalk from the Hard Rock Hotel & Casino and covers roughly 5.2 acres. A perpetual riparian grant allows the property to extend as far as 2,850 feet into the Atlantic Ocean. The existing pier footprint could also potentially be expanded by 25%.

Article Title: A 2,100-acre data-centre project was proposed near a Civil War battlefield park in Virginia; residents fought for years to stop it, ultimately ending the project
Article Text:
Henry Hill at Manassas National Battlefield Park in Prince William County Virginia

A 2,100-acre data-centre planned near Civil War history

Why residents and preservationists opposed it

The Bull Run Monument on Henry Hill is among the nation's earliest Civil War monuments.

County approves the project after a 27-hour hearing

Lawsuits challenge the county’s public notices

Developers withdraw from the legal battle

What happens to the land after the project’s end?

A major data-centre campus planned beside a historic Civil War battlefield in Virginia has been abandoned after years of community opposition and legal challenges. The Prince William Digital Gateway, proposed along Pageland Lane in Prince William County, would have brought up to 37 data-centre buildings to approximately 2,100 acres near Manassas National Battlefield Park. Residents, landowners and preservation groups challenged the project’s approvals, arguing that the development threatened the area’s historic character and raised broader concerns about large-scale infrastructure. In March 2026, the Virginia Court of Appeals upheld a ruling invalidating the project’s three rezonings over defective public notices. QTS Data Centers later withdrew its appeal, ending the proposal in July 2026.The Digital Gateway was designed as a large-scale technology campus in rural western Prince William County. QTS Data Centers and Compass Datacenters planned to develop the site, with the proposed facilities expected to total more than 22 million square feet at full build-out. QTS planned approximately 11.3 million square feet, while Compass proposed up to 11.55 million square feet. The completed campus would have included as many as 37 buildings and represented a multibillion-dollar investment in the region’s data-centre industry.The location was a central point of the controversy. The proposed site stood beside Manassas National Battlefield Park, which preserves the landscape of two major Civil War battles: the First Battle of Manassas, also known as the First Battle of Bull Run, fought on 21 July 1861, and the Second Battle of Manassas, also known as the Second Battle of Bull Run, fought from 28 to 30 August 1862. Preservationists argued that a major industrial development next to the park could damage the historic setting and views associated with the battlefield.Opposition came from local residents, landowners and organisations concerned about the proposed campus’s effect on the surrounding area. Critics raised questions about the development’s scale, its proximity to the battlefield and the possible consequences for the rural landscape. Environmental and infrastructure concerns also formed part of the wider debate surrounding the project.The American Battlefield Trust was among the groups challenging the development. Its opposition focused on protecting the historic landscape near Manassas National Battlefield Park. Residents also became involved in legal action against the county and the developers, arguing that the approvals had not followed the public-notice requirements established by law.The project had supporters as well. Developers said it would bring tens of billions of dollars in capital investment, substantial annual tax revenue and thousands of long-term jobs. The disagreement was therefore not limited to the question of construction near a historic site. It also involved competing views about economic development, land use and the future of data-centre infrastructure in Northern Virginia.The Prince William County Board of County Supervisors approved the three rezoning applications in December 2023. The decision followed a public meeting that lasted approximately 27 hours, during which residents and other participants debated the project.The rezonings were necessary to allow the proposed data-centre development on land that had previously been zoned for other uses. The approvals followed an earlier comprehensive plan amendment adopted by the county in November 2022. That amendment established a policy framework for potential data-centre development in the Digital Gateway area, while the later rezoning decisions addressed the specific properties involved in the project.Opponents subsequently filed lawsuits challenging the approvals. Their central legal argument concerned the county’s compliance with public-notice requirements before the December 2023 hearing. The case would eventually turn on that procedural issue rather than on a general legal ban on data centres near Civil War battlefields.In August 2025, Prince William Circuit Court Judge Kimberly A. Irving ruled that the rezonings were void because the county had failed to comply with the applicable public-notice requirements. The notices were required to be published in accordance with state law and the county’s zoning ordinance before the public hearing and vote.The case involved challenges brought by landowners, including the Oak Valley Homeowners Association, and the American Battlefield Trust. The plaintiffs argued that the deficiencies in the notices made the rezoning approvals legally invalid.The Virginia Court of Appeals upheld the ruling on 31 March 2026. The court found that the county’s advertising was deficient and affirmed the invalidation of the three rezonings. The decision concerned the legality of the approval process. It did not establish that all future data-centre proposals in the area would be prohibited.Following the appeals court’s decision, Prince William County and Compass Datacenters chose not to continue their appeals. QTS initially pursued a further challenge before the Virginia Supreme Court, making it the last developer seeking to preserve a legal route for the project.QTS eventually withdrew its appeal on 2 July 2026 and announced that it would terminate the Digital Gateway project. The decision ended the proposal after years of planning, public controversy and litigation.In its statement, QTS defended the original project, saying it had advanced through years of planning, analysis and public review. The company also pointed to the investment, tax revenue and employment it believed the development would have generated. Opponents welcomed the withdrawal, with preservation groups and community organisations describing it as a victory after years of campaigning and legal action.The termination of the Digital Gateway project does not permanently rule out future development proposals on the site. Prince William County said in an update published on 5 August 2026 that the three rezoning approvals were void and that the properties had reverted to their original zoning districts. The comprehensive plan amendment, however, remained in place.Any future attempt to rezone the properties would have to follow the normal application process, including review by county staff and public hearings before the Planning Commission and Board of County Supervisors. This means the end of the current project does not amount to a permanent prohibition on data-centre development in the wider area.
Article Summary: The Prince William Digital Gateway was designed as a large-scale technology campus in rural western Prince William County. The proposed site stood beside Manassas National Battlefield Park, which preserves the landscape of two major Civil War battles. Critics raised questions about the development’s scale, its proximity to the battlefield and the possible consequences for the rural landscape.

Article Title: Video: US forces take out floating refueling station allegedly linked to drug trafficking
Article Text:
US forces intercepted and cleared the vessel before removing its crew. The individuals taken from the vessel were subsequently transferred to Ecuadorian authorities, Southcom said in a statement.

Vessel allegedly supported drug trafficking

Ecuadorian authorities involved

US joint task force western Hemisphere (JTF-WHEM) forces on September 16 intercepted a floating refuelling station in the Eastern Pacific that was allegedly supporting illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations, the US southern command (Southcom) said, adding that the vessel had been linked through intelligence to Ecuador's Los Choneros organisation.In a video released by the Southcom, the joint task force can be seen striking the vessel as US forces board the vessel to conduct raid.The operation was conducted under the direction of Southcom as part of efforts to disrupt the logistical networks used to support drug trafficking operations in the Western Hemisphere.US forces intercepted and cleared the vessel before removing its crew. The individuals taken from the vessel were subsequently transferred to Ecuadorian authorities, Southcom said in a statement.After the crew had disembarked and the vessel had been cleared, US forces sank the floating refuelling station.According to Southcom, intelligence had established the vessel's involvement with Los Choneros, an Ecuadorian criminal organisation that US authorities describe as a violent narco-terrorist organisation.The refuelling station's role was significant because such vessels can provide logistical support to boats operating at sea, allowing them to continue travelling without returning frequently to shore for fuel.Southcom did not provide details on the amount of fuel involved, the duration of the vessel's alleged support to trafficking operations or the quantity of drugs, if any, seized during the operation.The command also did not disclose the location of the interception beyond identifying the Eastern Pacific as the area of the operation.The operation involved cooperation between US and Ecuadorian authorities. People removed from the vessel were handed over to Ecuadorian authorities after the US forces intercepted it.Southcom said the operation was aimed at weakening the wider logistical infrastructure that enables maritime drug trafficking rather than targeting only individual trafficking boats."Alongside our Ecuadorian partners, we are relentlessly pursuing narco-terrorists who prey on our citizens, undermine hemispheric security, and leave death and suffering in their wake. This deliberate, lawful, and precise operation saves lives and makes our citizens—from Ecuador to the United States—safer." - Southcom Commander General Francis L. DonovanSouthcom said JTF-WHEM would continue to conduct operations designed to dismantle logistical networks supporting narco-trafficking across the Western Hemisphere.The operation comes amid broader US efforts to work with regional partners against drug-trafficking networks operating across the Americas. In this case, the US command specifically identified Los Choneros as the organisation connected to the intercepted vessel.No further details about weapons used during the operation, casualties or any separate strike were provided in the Southcom statement.
Article Summary: US forces intercepted and cleared the vessel before removing its crew. The individuals taken from the vessel were subsequently transferred to Ecuadorian authorities. The vessel had been linked through intelligence to Ecuador's Los Choneros organisation. US forces sank the floating refuelling station after the crew had disembarked.

Article Title: In 1976, Minnesota residents fought plans for landfills and development along their river valley; 50 years later, the refuge they helped create protects more than 15,000 acres
Article Text:
Conservation challenges remain part of the conversation and the anniversary panel will examine issues facing the Minnesota River Valley, including water quality, flooding and development along the river's bluffs.

A half-century of protection

Monarchs make their seasonal journey

A new symbol for Minnesota parks

Half a century ago, a stretch of Minnesota river country faced a very different future. Plans for landfills and development threatened the Minnesota River bottoms, prompting local residents to push back against a transformation they believed would erase one of the region's most valuable natural landscapes. Today, that fight has left behind an urban wilderness stretching for miles, giving wildlife a protected corridor surprisingly close to the Twin Cities, reports The Minnesota Star Tribune.According to The Minnesota Star Tribune, the Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge is marking 50 years since the land came under federal protection through the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The refuge now spans more than 15,000 acres along roughly 50 miles of trails and river habitat, stretching from Bloomington to Henderson. Its forests, wetlands, grasslands and river bottoms provide space for birds, insects and other wildlife while giving residents access to nature in a heavily developed part of the state. A 50th anniversary celebration is planned for Sept. 26 at the refuge's visitor center in Bloomington. The event will include a panel featuring current and former refuge managers, along with activities such as archery and a bird walk beginning at 8 a.m.,adds the report. Conservation challenges remain part of the conversation and the anniversary panel will examine issues facing the Minnesota River Valley, including water quality, flooding and development along the river's bluffs.The anniversary comes as another natural spectacle unfolds across Minnesota. Monarch butterflies are currently moving through the state on their annual migration toward Mexico. From the North Shore to the Minnesota River Valley, large numbers of monarchs have been spotted, particularly around blazing stars, a late-summer favorite for the butterflies. People hoping to follow the migration can turn to the Project Monarch app and the citizen-science website Journey North, which track sightings and migration activity. Another chance to see the insects is coming Sept. 18, when Gooseberry Falls State Park hosts a Pollinator Party from 10 a.m. to noon. Recent sightings around Two Harbors included thousands of monarchs. The event will also highlight other pollinators and insects, including bumblebees, parasitic wasps and soldier beetles.The state's natural landscapes are also getting a chance to appear on the road. The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources is accepting designs for a new state parks license plate through Oct. 31. Entrants have been asked to incorporate the North Shore and Lake Superior agate, Minnesota's official state gemstone, into their designs. Once submissions close, a panel will choose three finalists. For a state that has spent decades balancing development with conservation, the license plate contest offers a small reminder of how closely Minnesota's identity remains tied to its parks, waterways and wild spaces.Image Courtesy: istock
Article Summary: The Minnesota Valley National Wildlife Refuge is marking 50 years since the land came under federal protection. The refuge now spans more than 15,000 acres along roughly 50 miles of trails and river habitat. A 50th anniversary celebration is planned for Sept. 26 at the refuge's visitor center in Bloomington.

Article Title: In 2013, St Agnes and Gugh began removing invasive rats brought by 18th-century shipwrecks; 12 years later, Manx shearwater breeding sites rose from 22 to a record 225
Article Text:
In the latest 2025 monitoring data, St Agnes and Gugh recorded 225 apparently occupied breeding sites (AOBs) for Manx shearwaters

Rats posed threat

Lesser black-backed gull chick at a coastal sub-colony on Gugh

Seabird breeding increased

Rat-free islands

In 2013, a major conservation effort began on St Agnes and Gugh in the Isles of Scilly to remove brown rats that had been harming nesting seabirds. According to the Isles of Scilly Wildlife Trust, the rats had arrived on the islands following shipwrecks in the 18th century and had become a threat to birds that nested in burrows, including Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels.For this, the Isles of Scilly Seabird Recovery Project was started which brought together local residents, conservationists and wildlife specialists who worked with Wildlife Management International Ltd (WMIL) to look for rat nests and signs of activity before the removal programme began.The intensive baiting operation started in November, 2013. Bait was placed across the islands and monitored every day, with teams checking how much was being taken. By the end of the month, the last evidence of rats had been recorded, but further monitoring continued to make sure the animals had not survived or returned.The recovery of the seabirds has since been tracked through regular surveys. In the latest 2025 monitoring data, St Agnes and Gugh recorded 225 apparently occupied breeding sites (AOBs) for Manx shearwaters, the highest number recorded there. Before the rat removal project, the number of Manx shearwater pairs stood at 22.Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels are particularly vulnerable to rats because they breed in burrows. Nests can be unsuccessful when rats are present, making invasive predators a major barrier to the recovery of these seabird populations.The islands are home to 13 species of breeding seabirds, with about 17,000 individual birds. The UK holds most of the world's population of both European storm petrels and Manx shearwaters.Before the project, seabird numbers had been declining for years. The removal programme therefore focused on eliminating the brown rats from St Agnes and Gugh rather than simply reducing their numbers. The project says this approach has been used on more than 700 islands worldwide.The first signs of recovery appeared soon after the rats were removed. Conservationists reported that Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels successfully bred on the islands for the first time in living memory. More than 40 chicks of the two species were recorded during the first two years following the removal.The latest monitoring shows that the recovery has continued for Manx shearwaters. There were 22 Manx shearwater pairs before the 2013 project. More than 10 years after rat eradication, there are now almost 200 pairs, while the 2025 monitoring recorded 225 apparently occupied breeding sites.The 2025 survey also found changes in other seabird populations on St Agnes and Gugh. The lesser black-backed gull colony increased slightly to 491 pairs, its highest level since 2014. The kittiwake colony also had 32 apparently occupied nests, which was more than the previous year, although observed breeding success was lower. Signs of cat predation of storm petrels were also recorded.St Agnes and Gugh have remained rat-free since the eradication carried out during the winter of 2013-14. Regular monitoring continues to check for any signs that rats have returned. The islands were officially declared rat-free in early 2017 after further checks. A biosecurity detection dog also visited the islands in February 2025 as part of checks for any returning rats.The islands also faced a possible mouse issue during the winter of 2024. Probable signs were found in chicken feed, prompting four months of monitoring. However, no further signs were found and the team concluded that the mouse had probably died or left before the chicken feed arrived on St Agnes.The success on St Agnes and Gugh has also led conservation groups to consider rat eradication on other islands. A new project is being developed for St Martin's, Tresco, Bryher and about 21 nearby uninhabited islands. Because the islands are closely connected, the proposed operation would need to take place across the whole area at the same time. Since 2025, the team has also held co-design workshops and open days to involve island communities in planning the work.
Article Summary: Brown rats had been harming nesting seabirds on St Agnes and Gugh. They arrived on the islands following shipwrecks in the 18th century. They had become a threat to birds that nested in burrows, including Manx shearwaters and European storm petrels. The islands are home to 13 species of breeding seabird, with about 17,000 individual birds.

Article Title: In 1976, Buffalo turned a 264-acre industrial dump into a nature preserve; 50 years later, its 75-acre marsh is Erie County’s largest remnant wetland and 260+ bird species have been observed
Article Text:
Buffalo turned a 264-acre industrial dump into a nature preserve; 50 years later, its 75-acre marsh is Erie County’s largest remnant wetland (Image Credit: Tifft Nature Preserve)

From industrial land to protected nature preserve

The site now includes a 75-acre cattail marsh, while more than 260 bird species have been observed there (Image Credit: Tifft Nature Preserve)

A wetland survives within Buffalo

Decades of restoration and ecological research

A 50-year transformation continues

A former industrial site and municipal landfill on Buffalo’s Outer Harbor has spent the past five decades becoming something very different: a 264-acre urban nature preserve supporting wetlands, woodlands, ponds and diverse wildlife. Tifft Nature Preserve, which officially became a nature preserve in 1976, is marking its 50th anniversary in 2026. According to Tifft Nature Preserve, the site now includes a 75-acre cattail marsh, while more than 260 bird species have been observed there. Its transformation involved covering buried waste, restoring habitat and establishing long-term ecological management and research.The land that became Tifft Nature Preserve had a much longer history before it became a protected natural area. According to the preserve, it was once part of a large dairy farm owned by George Washington Tifft before becoming a transshipment centre for commodities including coal and iron ore. As Buffalo's industrial activity expanded, portions of the property were used for various forms of waste and fill.During the 1950s and 1960s, the City of Buffalo acquired the property and used it as a dumpsite for municipal refuse. The site therefore entered the 1970s with an industrial and waste-management legacy rather than as an untouched natural landscape.The future of the remaining habitat changed when concerned citizens pushed for the site's ecological value to be recognised. A 1975 master plan laid out plans for trails, ecological management and administration, while the city restricted refuse transfer to the southwest portion of the property. The land began its transition towards becoming a nature preserve.In the 1970s, nearly two million cubic feet of solid municipal waste was enclosed in clay and covered with soil excavated from another part of the property. Ponds were enlarged, trees and wildflowers were planted, and efforts were made to protect the site's large cattail marsh. In 1976, the area officially became Tifft Farm Nature Preserve.One of the most important parts of the preserve is its 75-acre cattail marsh. Tifft describes the marsh as a remnant of a much larger wetland complex that once extended across parts of the surrounding region. Its survival gives the preserve particular ecological importance within an increasingly urban landscape. The marsh is also central to Tifft's wildlife value. The preserve's research programme notes that more than 260 bird species have been observed there, while its location along Lake Erie provides opportunities for studying wildlife associated with wetlands and waterfront habitats. Tifft has also been designated an Important Bird Area by the National Audubon Society.The habitat has not simply been left to develop without intervention. Ecological management has included efforts to control invasive plants, create open-water habitat and increase native vegetation. In 1999, canals were dredged to create additional open-water areas for waterfowl and marsh birds. Later projects expanded ponds and addressed invasive species affecting the marsh.Tifft's transformation has continued long after its designation as a preserve. In 1982, the Buffalo Society of Natural Sciences took charge of the city-owned property, and the preserve became what the organisation describes as a “living collection” containing vegetation, wildlife, hydrology, soils, natural processes and history.Research expanded substantially over subsequent decades. The preserve has worked with students and faculty from institutions including Buffalo State College, Canisius College, SUNY Buffalo, SUNY Fredonia, SUNY Geneseo and Erie County Community College. Research has covered subjects ranging from invasive species and wetland management to wildlife and environmental science.The ecological work has included large-scale habitat projects. Between 2009 and 2014, more than 2,100 trees representing 29 native species were planted as part of a tree regeneration project. In 2011 and subsequent years, management of invasive Phragmites in the marsh helped create conditions for native wetland vegetation, followed by the planting of more than 30,000 native emergent and floating aquatic plants. More recently, an 18-acre area around the East Canal has been undergoing ecological renovation, including invasive-species removal, native plant establishment and efforts to improve habitat and water quality.Tifft's 50th anniversary in 2026 marks more than the passage of time. It represents a long transition from industrial and waste-related land use to a site focused on conservation, research and public access. The preserve now has about five miles of nature trails, boardwalks and viewing areas around its wetlands and other habitats. During its anniversary year, Tifft also opened a three-quarter-mile accessible trail and rebuilt an accessible boardwalk through the cattail marsh, expanding opportunities for visitors to experience the site.The transformation has not erased every environmental challenge. Tifft continues to manage invasive species and other ecological pressures, while its current research programme examines the preserve's soils, wildlife, vegetation and broader environmental conditions. In 2025, the preserve also reported a potential sheen and odour at an on-site creek, leading to environmental sampling by the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation and other agencies.Yet the broader trajectory is striking. Land that once handled industrial materials and municipal refuse now supports a large cattail marsh, wooded areas, ponds and hundreds of recorded bird species. Tifft Nature Preserve's history shows how an urban landscape with a heavily altered past can be managed over decades to create a functioning habitat and a place for scientific research, environmental education and public access.
Article Summary: Tifft Nature Preserve is a 264-acre urban nature preserve in Buffalo, New York. The site includes a 75-acre cattail marsh, while more than 260 bird species have been observed there. The preserve has been designated an Important Bird Area by the National Audubon Society. It marks its 50th anniversary in 2026.

Article Title: Trump to meet Gulf leaders at UN over Iran war, postwar strategy: Report
Article Text:
The US state department sent out initial invitations on Wednesday, the report said. The meeting could also be expanded to include other Arab and Muslim leaders.

Why the meeting matters

Netanyahu also seeks Trump meeting

What happened last year

US President Donald Trump is expected to meet leaders and foreign ministers from Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries in New York next Tuesday to discuss the next steps in the war with Iran. The meeting is expected to focus on US plans for the postwar period, three sources with direct knowledge told Axios.The meeting is likely to bring together representatives from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman on the sidelines of the UN general assembly.The US state department sent out initial invitations on Wednesday, the report said. The meeting could also be expanded to include other Arab and Muslim leaders.The Gulf states have been directly affected by the conflict. Countries that host US military bases came under major Iranian attacks during the war.The fighting has also caused significant economic disruption in the region, including losses linked to interruptions in oil and natural gas exports.Trump and his senior team are working on a plan for what happens after the war. According to the report, the postwar strategy is expected to be finalised after the US midterm elections.Trump said on Wednesday that "hopefully we are towards the end of the war."He also repeated his claim that Iran wants to reach a deal, saying the US had heard this directly from Tehran.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also wants to meet Trump in New York, but no meeting has been scheduled, an Israeli source said.The development comes as Washington continues to consider its approach to the next phase of the conflict and the wider regional consequences of the war.The planned Gulf meeting also recalls Trump's diplomacy during last year's UN General Assembly.At the time, Trump met leaders from eight Arab and Muslim countries and presented them with a draft plan for ending the Gaza war.He made the plan public a week later. A deal to end the war was reached shortly afterwards.The White House has declined to comment on the planned meeting with the Gulf leaders.

Article Title: Meet Austin Jin, the 16-year-old Great Neck, New York student who built a CRISPR blood test to detect tuberculosis and drug resistance; he won $50,000
Article Text:
Outside the lab, Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter. He also co-founded Project LIFE, a student-led initiative that has grown to over 20 chapters in eight states, with a mission to improve education and access to the bone marrow registry.

Another approach to TB diagnosis

Drug resistance testing

Research to broader impact

Most teenagers go to a pathology office for a blood test. For Austin Jin, it was the launch pad to address one of medicine’s oldest and most enduring problems: diagnosing tuberculosis. A 16-year-old senior at William A. Shine Great Neck South High School in Great Neck, NY, developed M-CATCH, a diagnostic platform based on CRISPR that can detect tuberculosis from blood and identify drug-resistant strains. According to the Davidson Institute website, his work earned him the 2026 Davidson Fellowship and a $50,000 scholarship. Scroll down to read about his journey.Tuberculosis remains a major global health threat with over a million deaths reported annually worldwide. But one of the biggest challenges in fighting the disease comes even before treatment starts: getting an accurate diagnosis. Sputum, the mucus produced deep in the lungs, is used in many standard TB tests. And that creates a particular problem for young children and severely ill or immunocompromised patients, many of whom have difficulty producing a usable sample.But in the online report, Jin’s project takes a different tack.M-CATCH screens the blood serum for circulating bacterial DNA fragments in the blood. The system uses polymerase chain reactions and CRISPR-Cas12a technology to find genetic signatures associated with tuberculosis.This test is not intended to determine whether tuberculosis exists. It can also look for genetic alterations that make the bacteria resistant to certain drugs and that level of detection can come down to a single change in DNA. Jin engineered CRISPR guide RNAs that can distinguish between these tiny genetic differences and combined them with a microfluidics chip that allows multiple reactions to occur at the same time.The result is a multiplex platform that can screen hundreds of reactions for more than one mutation simultaneously. This could eventually make large-scale testing more practical, especially in places where sophisticated laboratories are not readily available.The path to the finished system had its challenges. Designing good CRISPR guide RNAs was particularly tricky because many candidates that looked good on paper did not work as expected in experiments. Jin had spent weeks testing and tweaking them. He’s interested in more than tuberculosis. He plans to major in biomedical engineering and biochemistry to prepare for a career as a physician-scientist, with the hope of translating laboratory research into useful tools for medicine.Outside the lab, Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter. He also co-founded Project LIFE, a student-led initiative that has grown to over 20 chapters in eight states, with a mission to improve education and access to the bone marrow registry.His M-CATCH platform could eventually be adapted to detect other infectious diseases and possibly even cancer, suggesting a future where a small blood sample could reveal far more than a single diagnosis.Images Courtesy: Davidson Institute
Article Summary: Austin Jin, 16, developed M-CATCH, a diagnostic platform based on CRISPR that can detect tuberculosis from blood and identify drug-resistant strains. His work earned him the 2026 Davidson Fellowship and a $50,000 scholarship. Jin captains his varsity swim team and co-presidents his DECA chapter.

Article Title: 'Hostile act': Trump livid as EU mulls making Canada its first 'associate member'
Article Text:
" ... If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," Trump said.

Canada seeks closer ties with Europe amid US tensions

What would closer EU-Canada ties cover

Trump dismisses proposal and threatens tariffs

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think of threat by Trump to impose tariffs on Europe? It's a necessary move to protect US interests. It's counterproductive to global trade. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose heavy tariffs on Europe after the European Union proposed giving Canada a new form of membership, in a move that could bring the two sides closer on trade, defence and economic security.European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen made the proposal during her annual State of the European Union address on Wednesday, telling Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney that she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.Trump reacted sharply to the proposal, suggesting that the EU's plan could be a "hostile act" and warning that the US could respond with higher tariffs on European goods."If it's a good intention, that's fine. If it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe," Trump said, while also suggesting that the US could restrict trade with Europe in certain areas.The proposal comes as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States following Trump's tariffs and repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state.Carney has called for a "unique alliance" with the EU as Ottawa seeks stronger economic and security ties with Europe.Von der Leyen said the EU and Canada would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, through a wider partnership called the "Alliance for the Future". The proposed arrangement would aim to create "a common prosperity and economic security space."Carney received a standing ovation from European lawmakers after von der Leyen's address. He is scheduled to speak to the European Parliament on Thursday.The European Commission president said the proposed partnership would go beyond trade and be based on shared democratic values."I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen told Carney."Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen said. "We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."The expanded relationship would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defence production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security."This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she said. "In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible."Trump called the prospect of Canada joining the EU "laughable" and described Canada as a "terrible trade partner".He said the US would assess the intentions of European leaders before deciding whether to impose further tariffs, leaving open the possibility of a broader trade confrontation.The EU's proposal does not amount to full EU membership for Canada. It is an offer to explore a closer relationship that would expand existing cooperation in trade, security and other areas.For Ottawa, the initiative offers a potential way to strengthen ties with Europe at a time when its relationship with Washington remains strained.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump has threatened to impose heavy tariffs on Europe. The EU has proposed giving Canada a new form of membership. The move could bring the two sides closer on trade, defence and economic security. Trump called the prospect of Canada joining the EU "laughable"

Article Title: At 22, Jayden Williams became Stockbridge’s youngest mayor; 10 months later, the city council removed him after a 10-hour misconduct hearing
Article Text:
Allegations of Financial Mismanagement

Lyft rides, haircuts and movie tickets

Personal clothing and tailoring services

Several restaurant visits and meal charges

Misuse of City Assets and Personnel

Defense Claims Personal Grudge

Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council voted to remove him from office following a 10-hour misconduct hearing focused on his administrative conduct, spending and use of city resources. According to local reports, Williams, now 23, was removed after the council reviewed evidence gathered during a months-long investigation. The council’s decision ended a difficult investigation into Williams’ use of public funds, city property and communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander has taken over as interim mayor while city officials prepare for a special election to fill the vacant position. Atlanta News First reported that the city is preparing a formal resolution declaring the mayor’s seat vacant.The hearing lasted from about 9:00 a.m. until nearly 9:00 p.m. City attorneys and investigators presented evidence about Williams’ handling of public money. A major part of the case involved allegations that Williams repeatedly used city purchasing cards for personal expenses. According to evidence presented during the hearing and reported by WSB-TV, the disputed charges included:Investigators also focused on a $322.92 charge made on Father’s Day at Pandora on the Square in McDonough.According to the city’s investigation documents, Williams originally listed the purchase as gift cards for city staff and later said the items had been given to community members. He also filed a form saying the original receipt was missing. Investigators later obtained the receipt. It showed that the $322.92 was spent on beverages and Father’s Day meals for Williams’ family, according to the evidence presented by the city.Williams defended himself during the hearing, saying he did not intentionally use the city card for personal purchases. He also argued that many of the disputed transactions were connected to official city business. WSB-TV reported that Williams said he reimbursed the city for some of the expenses. When questioned about Stockbridge’s purchasing and ethics policy, Williams testified that he had not read it. He said he had not received a copy when he took office, although he had asked for information about the rules after being elected. WSB-TV reported that Williams also maintained that he had not received proper training on the city’s policies.The investigation also examined Williams’ use of a city-owned vehicle and fuel cards. According to evidence presented during the hearing, Williams had a city vehicle checked out for 183 days between January and June. The city said this accounted for all but nine days of his early time in office. Local reporting also noted that the city’s rules require municipal vehicles to be used for official business or emergencies. Williams disputed the city’s interpretation of his vehicle use. Earlier, he said the vehicle remained available to him but that he was not necessarily using it every day. His attorney also argued that Williams had not received comprehensive training on the city’s vehicle policies. The city also presented evidence that Williams accumulated about $2,600 in fuel expenses using a city card during the same period, according to WSB-TV.The hearing also examined Williams’ communications with an 18-year-old high school student. Evidence presented to the council included text messages exchanged in late November and early December, before Williams took office, as well as additional messages sent in January. Reports said the communications included sexually suggestive messages and allegations involving explicit photographs. Police reviewed the communications but did not bring criminal charges. The student was 18 and therefore legally an adult under Georgia law. However, the city continued to examine the matter as a possible violation of the conduct standards expected of an elected official. Williams has said the communications took place before he became mayor. In a previous statement reported by FOX 5 Atlanta, he said the individual was 18 at the time and had never taken part in the city’s “Mayor for a Day” program. City Attorney Quinton Washington said the council considered the evidence as a whole before deciding to remove Williams. “When taken in concert together, the employee treatment, all of those things were things that they felt like did not uphold the standard that Stockbridge would like to see in its mayor,” Washington said.After the council’s vote, Mayor Pro Tem Elton Alexander defended the decision, saying officials had a responsibility to protect the city and its residents. “The results of the investigation demanded we act,” Alexander said. Alexander also confirmed that he does not plan to run in the special election to permanently replace Williams.“I have no desire to be mayor,” Alexander said. “For me to run for mayor means giving up my ability to vote, and I would never do that.” Williams and his attorney, Robert Kenner, strongly disagreed with the council’s decision. They argued that council members were biased against the mayor and had already made up their minds before the hearing.Kenner said the decision was not supported by sufficient evidence and accused the council of acting because of a personal dispute with Williams. “What happened tonight was very disappointing,” Kenner said. “I don’t believe that it was based on any evidence. I think it was based on a personal grudge against the mayor.”Kenner said Williams has the right to challenge the council’s decision in court. He indicated that the legal team would consider an appeal in Henry County Superior Court. The proceedings had already faced legal challenges before the final vote. Councilwoman LaKeisha Gantt was barred from participating after a judge found that her previous communications showed bias against Williams. The judge’s decision followed evidence involving messages and other communications between Gantt and people connected to the mayor.Gantt therefore did not take part in the final removal decision, according to CBS Atlanta. The city is now preparing for a special election to choose Williams’ replacement. Atlanta News First reported that officials are working on the formal steps needed to declare the mayor’s seat vacant and begin the election process. Officials are also expected to determine whether Williams will legally be allowed to run again.
Article Summary: Jayden Williams made history as the youngest mayor of Stockbridge when he took office at age 22 in January. Just 10 months later, the city council voted to remove him from office following a 10-hour misconduct hearing. The council’s decision ended a difficult investigation into Williams’ use of public funds, city property and communications with a high school student.

Article Title: In 1978, two boys digging in a Los Angeles yard found a buried Ferrari; Farmers Insurance recovered the three-year-hidden Dino and sold it through a special sealed-bid auction
Article Text:
Representative image of a vintage sports car being uncovered after years buried beneath a suburban backyard. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

The Ferrari disappeared in 1974

From buried car to insurance auction

Two boys digging in a Los Angeles yard unearthed a stolen Ferrari Dino 246 in 1978. Image Credits: Wikipedia.

The Dino returns to the road

Ordinary digging in a Los Angeles backyard in 1978 led to the discovery of a Ferrari that had been missing for more than three years. According to the Los Angeles Times, two boys playing in the backyard of a house on West 119th Street in Los Angeles were digging in the mud in February 1978 when they found something unusual just below the surface. They told sheriff’s deputies that it felt like the roof of a car. Investigators returned with a skid-steer loader and shovels and uncovered a green 1974 Ferrari, which had been reported stolen in December 1974. The car was found in good condition despite having been buried underground for more than three years.Rosendo Cruz of Alhambra bought the Dino in October 1974. Just two months later, on December 7, Cruz reported the Ferrari stolen, and Farmers Insurance reimbursed him for the loss. The theft report remained on file with the Los Angeles Police Department, but the car was missing from the record for more than three years.When the car was excavated, the discovery suggested that the vehicle had been deliberately buried, not abandoned. The Ferrari was thought to have been covered with rugs and other materials, even though some portions of the car remained uncovered in the moist soil. Although Southern California's relatively dry climate may have helped preserve some of the car, it still required restoration after spending years underground.The car was particularly significant because it was not just any Ferrari, but a Dino 246, a model known for its distinctive design and engineering. According to Motor Sport Magazine, the Ferrari Dino 246 GT was styled by Pininfarina and powered by a 2.4-litre, 65-degree V6 mounted transversely ahead of the rear wheels. The fixed-roof GT was followed in 1972 by the 246 GTS, a targa-style version with a detachable roof panel. The GTS retained the GT's basic mechanical layout while adding an open-air design.After the Ferrari was recovered, Farmers Insurance faced an unusual question: what should it do with a car that had already been paid out as a theft claim? Since the company had reimbursed the original owner, the recovered vehicle became its property. Rather than simply sell it through an ordinary used-car transaction, Farmers arranged a special sealed-bid auction. By then, the case was already well known, and potential buyers were eager to see the Ferrari. The auction process produced another twist. The car was shown to prospective buyers, but some parts appeared to go missing during the exhibition period. Farmers realised that many of the initial bids were not genuine. The eventual sale turned the buried Dino from an insurance recovery into a collector’s car with an extraordinary history. Its unusual past was now part of its appeal, alongside the Ferrari name and the rarity of the 246 GTS.It was not long until the car had gone through numerous owners and fell into the possession of Ferrari fanatic Brad Howard. After some time, the vehicle was restored. The work included mechanical repairs and cosmetic restoration. Giuseppe Cappalonga, who was an expert on Ferraris, worked on restoring the vehicle. The restoration appears to have preserved the Ferrari’s unusual history. It went from being reported stolen in 1974 to being recovered in 1978, auctioned by the insurer, and eventually restored by collectors. The restoration did not wipe away the Dino’s past. Instead, it put the car back on the road while leaving its unusual history intact. From being stolen and buried to being found years later and restored, the Dino had already lived through more than most classic cars ever do. Its survival became part of what made the Ferrari so memorable.
Article Summary: Two boys digging in a Los Angeles yard unearthed a stolen Ferrari Dino 246 in 1978. The green 1974 Ferrari had been reported stolen in December 1974. The car was found in good condition despite having been buried underground for more than three years. It went from being reported stolen to being recovered in 1978, auctioned by the insurer, and eventually restored.

Article Title: ISIS-inspired shooting suspect identified as former Reddit moderator
Article Text:
The U.S. Department of Justice logo (Photo: AP)

How did the FBI track Kramer before his arrest?

‘Preparing for my mission’: What investigators found online

FBI traces more Reddit activity to Kramer

What happened in Kramer’s earlier juvenile case?

A man accused of preparing an ISIS-inspired mass shooting was identified in a social-media post as a former moderator of r/doordash, Reddit’s community for the food-delivery platform DoorDash. The account operated under the username “u/i_love_femboys6969”. Federal records identify its user as Jonathan Hunter Kramer, 21, of Valencia, Pennsylvania.Investigators tied the account to Kramer through login credentials recovered from his laptop and Reddit subscriber records associated with his email address and phone number.Polymarket highlighted the r/doordash moderator connection. The federal affidavit does not itself identify r/doordash, though it records “u/i_love_femboys6969” saying it was “open to moderating any subreddit”.The Reddit activity formed one part of a broader federal investigation that culminated in Kramer’s arrest in September.Kramer faces a federal firearms charge over allegations that he received a gun and ammunition knowing, or having reason to believe, they would be used in a felony or terrorism offence. Prosecutors say the alleged terrorism conduct involved providing, attempting to provide or conspiring to provide material support to ISIS.Agents tracking Kramer on September 12 followed him from his home to a Walmart, where he bought a disposable phone. He later met another person outside the store and took possession of an elongated black bag from that person’s vehicle; an FBI agent believed it was large enough to contain a rifle.Kramer then travelled to a hotel in Cranberry Township and booked a week-long stay with cash. He later visited a sporting-goods shop before returning to the hotel, where agents approached him.The searches that followed uncovered about 190 rounds of rifle ammunition, a semiautomatic rifle and five magazines, along with a scope, bipod and pepper spray, investigators said. About 30 knives were recovered separately from Kramer’s residence. Federal agents arrested him after the searches.Investigators were also examining another strand of Kramer’s alleged online activity — a SimpleX user calling himself “Hamza Al Rashid”. The FBI linked the persona to Kramer after comparing the account’s activity with other information gathered during the investigation.On September 9, three days before Kramer’s arrest, “Hamza Al Rashid” wrote that he was “preparing for my mission” and indicated that obtaining a weapon was the remaining step before he would be ready.The account had also allegedly discussed an attack on a crowd with an FBI confidential human source, including the possible use of smoke and pepper grenades. Investigators separately found that Kramer had previously purchased pepper spray online.Authorities further allege that “Hamza Al Rashid” expressed support for ISIS and communicated with others about attacks and violent material. The persona was also linked to a SimpleX group called “The Brotherhood”, which investigators say was run by “Hamza Al Rashid”.The investigation into Kramer’s online footprint extended beyond the “Hamza Al Rashid” persona.Investigators identified “u/slopdestroyer” as an alternate Reddit account after “u/i_love_femboys6969” referred to it that way. Posts associated with the second account included material showing ISIS fighters or supporters and an ISIS nasheed.Agents also found overlap between the Reddit activity and the SimpleX account. In July, “u/i_love_femboys6969” recommended the encrypted messaging service SimpleX, while “Hamza Al Rashid” separately promoted the same platform as a secure means of communication.The September investigation was not Kramer’s first contact with law enforcement.He had come to authorities’ attention as a juvenile in 2023 over an alleged mass-casualty plot. The Justice Department says he was later adjudicated delinquent for his role in that case and for possession of child sexual abuse material. During the same investigation, an FBI agent said a recording recovered from Kramer’s laptop depicted what the agent described as a pledge of allegiance to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi.After Kramer was released from a Pennsylvania juvenile facility in March 2026, the FBI received another tip raising concerns about his online behaviour and renewed contact with people he had known before the earlier case. That tip helped set in motion the investigation that eventually led agents back to his online accounts and, months later, to his arrest.The current case remains at the criminal-complaint stage and the accusations have not been adjudicated. Kramer retains the presumption of innocence. He appeared in federal court on September 14. Prosecutors are seeking to keep him in custody while the case proceeds, citing what they describe as a threat to public safety.
Article Summary: Jonathan Hunter Kramer, 21, of Valencia, Pennsylvania, was arrested in September. He faces a federal firearms charge over allegations he received a gun and ammunition knowing, or having reason to believe, they would be used in a felony or terrorism offence. Prosecutors say the alleged terrorism conduct involved providing, attempting to provide or conspiring to provide material support to ISIS.

Article Title: In 2015, a Florida family followed a metal-detector signal beneath shallow sand and found 51 gold coins and a 40-foot gold chain from a 1715 wreck, worth over $1 million
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: Treasure hunters search shallow waters off Florida’s Treasure Coast for remnants of the 1715 Spanish Fleet | CHATGPT

A fleet caught in a hurricane

AI REPRESENTATION: Treasure hunters search shallow waters off Florida’s Treasure Coast for remnants of the 1715 Spanish Fleet | CHATGPT

The coin that stood out

A 1715 Spanish Fleet shipwreck site off Florida, alongside gold coins recovered from the historic wreck | Wikimedia Commons

A discovery timed to history

Another piece of a 300-year-old Spanish treasure story in 2015 was recovered off the Florida coast, when the Schmitt family recovered 51 gold coins and about 40 feet of ornate gold chain from the wreck of the flagship of Spain’s 1715 treasure fleet, Capitana. The haul was valued at more than $1 million and included a rare 1715 Royal Mexico Eight Escudos coin known as the “Tricentennial Royal.” TIME reported that the Schmitt family, who were professional treasure hunters working as subcontractors for 1715 Fleet-Queens Jewels LLC, had discovered the treasure off Florida’s coast.The Capitana was part of a Spanish fleet that was carrying gold, silver, and other valuable cargo from the Americas toward Spain. On July 30 and 31, 1715, the ships were caught in a hurricane while sailing past the Florida coast. National Geographic reported that 11 of the fleet’s 12 ships were lost during the storm, and scattered their cargo along the coastline. The wrecks subsequently became targets for generations of salvors and treasure hunters. The Capitana was among the vessels searched repeatedly, and modern recovery operations eventually brought individual coins and other artifacts back to the surface.The Schmitt family had already been involved in searching the 1715 wrecks for years, and TIME reported that the family had first found gold in 2013. Their later discovery from the Capitana became one of the more notable recoveries from the wreck because of both the number of gold coins and the unusual piece of jewelry found with them.The centerpiece of the recovery was a Royal Mexico Eight Escudos dated 1715, a coin that was struck during the same year the fleet was lost. It became known as the “Tricentennial Royal” because its recovery came roughly 300 years after it was made and lost at sea. TIME reported that the rare coin alone was valued at more than $500,000. The rest of the haul included dozens of other gold coins and a long, ornate gold chain. The Numismatic Guaranty Company documented the 2015 recovery and gives the date as June 18, 2015. It records the find as 51 gold coins and 40 feet of ornate gold chain, with the Tricentennial Royal identified as the centerpiece. Most of the recovered coins were minted in Lima, Peru, and included eight- and two-escudo denominations, which also illustrates why shipwreck coins can be valuable beyond their gold content.The recovery was made public in July 2015, rather than immediately after the find. National Geographic reported that the discovery had been made in June and that the Schmitt family waited to announce it so the news would coincide with the 300th anniversary of the fleet’s sinking. The divers were working in about 15 feet of water roughly 1,000 feet from a beach near Fort Pierce, Florida. Three centuries earlier, the hurricane had scattered the fleet and its cargo along the Florida coast, and in 2015, the anniversary brought attention back to the same wreck site as divers recovered objects that had remained buried beneath the seabed for generations.The NGC record shows that the Capitana produced another major recovery later that summer, when 350 gold coins were recovered on July 30 and 31, exactly 300 years after the fleet’s destruction. For the Schmitt family, however, the earlier June recovery remained particularly notable since the combination of 51 gold coins, a 40-foot chain, and a rare 1715 Royal turned a section of Florida’s seabed into a time capsule from one of Spain’s most famous treasure fleets.
Article Summary: The Schmitt family recovered 51 gold coins and about 40 feet of ornate gold chain from the wreck of the flagship of Spain's 1715 treasure fleet, Capitana. The haul was valued at more than $1 million and included a rare 1715 Royal Mexico Eight Escudos coin known as the “Tricentennial Royal.” The Capitanas were part of a Spanish fleet that was carrying gold, silver, and other valuable cargo from the Americas toward Spain.

Article Title: In 1984, a meteorite crushed the back of a Georgia woman’s steel mailbox and knocked it over; the battered mailbox later sold at auction for $83,000
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: A meteorite-damaged mailbox in rural Georgia, illustrating the unusual 1984 impact | ChatGPT

The night a space rock hit the mailbox

AI REPRESENTATION: A meteorite-damaged mailbox in rural Georgia, illustrating the unusual 1984 impact | ChatGPT

From rural mailbox to collector’s object

The L type ordinary chondrites are the second most common group of meteorites | Wikimedia Commons

The $82,750 auction surprise

A rural mailbox in Claxton, Georgia, was struck by a meteorite on December 10, 1984. The impact damaged the metal box and tore it from its wooden post, and left behind an object that would eventually become a curiosity in the world of meteorite collecting. In 2007, the battered mailbox was sold at a Bonhams auction for $82,750, including the buyer’s premium.The event occurred in the evening in Claxton, where the meteorite came down in Evans County. The Arizona State University Buseck Center for Meteorite Studies identifies the object as the Claxton meteorite, an L6 ordinary chondrite. Its account says witnesses heard a whistling sound followed by a crash and a thud as the rock fell. The meteorite was later estimated to have weighed about three pounds, with roughly 1,455 grams recovered. It struck the metal mailbox that belonged to Carutha Barnard and left a depression in the surrounding ground.The ASU meteorite center notes that the mailbox was later acquired by meteorite collector and tektite expert Hal Povenmire. A staged photograph from the period shows Barnard alongside Povenmire and the damaged mailbox, although the archive notes that the photograph was staged and that the mailbox had actually been torn from its post during the impact.The mailbox might have remained a local curiosity if the meteorite itself had not been recognized and preserved, but its connection to a documented extraterrestrial impact made the battered steel box rather unusual. The Claxton meteorite is significant because scientists were able to document the fall and recover pieces of the object. The ASU archive records that the stone was covered by a thin black fusion crust, which is a surface formed as the meteorite heated while passing through Earth’s atmosphere.The mailbox therefore became physical evidence of the event; its dents and damage were linked to a documented meteorite fall. The object had become something far removed from its original purpose by the time it reached auction, and was no longer being valued as a mailbox but as an artifact deeply associated with a rare astronomical event.The mailbox was offered at Bonhams in 2007 during an auction devoted to meteorites and related material. The sale included far more scientifically significant rocks, including pieces of famous meteorites, but the damaged Georgia mailbox became one of the unexpected highlights. The Associated Press reported that the mailbox sold for $82,750, including a 20% buyer’s premium. A small piece of the Claxton meteorite itself, weighing less than an ounce, sold separately for $7,700. The Smithsonian also highlighted the mailbox after the auction and described it as a battered metal box from Georgia that had been struck by a falling meteorite in 1984. Its final bid was reported as $82,750.The price tells us something unusual about meteorite collecting: sometimes the object connected to a meteorite can become nearly as interesting to collectors as the rock itself. The Claxton mailbox’s value came later, from the story attached to its damaged metal surface. A meteorite had crossed the atmosphere, struck the ground, and hit a household object that most tend to overlook. That accident transformed a rural mailbox into a documented piece of meteorite history, and decades later, into an auction item worth tens of thousands of dollars.
Article Summary: A rural mailbox in Claxton, Georgia, was struck by a meteorite on December 10, 1984. The impact damaged the metal box and tore it from its wooden post. In 2007, the mailbox was sold at a Bonhams auction for $82,750, including the buyer’s premium.

Article Title: In 1799, a 12-year-old found a 17-pound gold rock in a North Carolina creek; used as a doorstop for 3 years, it sold for $3.50 and sparked America’s first gold rush
Article Text:
AI Representation: A 17-pound gold rock worth $3,600 of gold in a North Carolina creek. Image credits: Chatgpt

John Reed, born Johannes Reith, settled in Cabarrus County

Conrad Reed finds a 17-pound rock in Little Meadow Creek, 1799

Reed forms a four-man mining partnership, 1803

Cabarrus/Stanly County Line on North Carolina Highway 73 in North Carolina. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Underground quartz mining begins at Reed's property, 1831

Reed Gold Mine became a

National Historic Landmark

In 1799, when a boy of 12 years old, named Conrad Reed was playing in Little Meadow Creek, located within Cabarrus County, North Carolina, he unearthed a heavy golden stone weighing 17 pounds and brought it home to show his father, John Reed, who was a farmer. Neither John nor his son knew the value of the stone, and the two spent the following three years living with it without realizing its importance and how important it would prove to be for their lives. The heavy stone served as a doorstop in their family house. Once the stone was identified as gold, it became part of a discovery that made North Carolina the country's leading gold producer for nearly 50 years, until the start of the California gold rush.The story of John Reed, who was actually born as Johannes Reith, was rather a peculiar one. He was a Hessian soldier in the British Army during the American Revolutionary War and at its end, he deserted and settled down amongst the German-speaking community in the Piedmont area of North Carolina, according to the North Carolina Division of State Historic Sites . He anglicized his name and took up farming, raising corn and wheat.This stone might definitely have remained unnoticed if Conrad had not discovered it in Little Meadow Creek in 1799 because of the unusual nature of the rock itself. Neither Conrad nor his father had known the rock's worth until three years later, when a jeweler realized it was gold. It was in 1802 that the mystery was solved when John Reed brought the rock to the jeweler in Fayetteville during his usual trip selling agricultural products. The jeweler recognized the rock as gold, worth roughly a thousand times what he then offered for it, and asked Reed to name his price. Unaware of the rock's true value, Reed asked for what he thought was a generous sum: $3.50, about a week's wages for a farmer at the time.Reed believed that there were more deposits of gold in the vicinity after becoming aware of the sale. In the year following this incident, Reed brought in three partners to form a mining company, making four men in total; in exchange for half the land and profits, they provided him with tools and laborers. The following year, a boy named Peter, who was enslaved, found a 28-pound gold nugget. According to the North Carolina Division of State Historic Sites, this is the biggest nugget found at the Reed Gold Mine. The discovery soon attracted the attention of Reed's neighbors.According to records in The Western Carolinian newspaper dated 1825, gold mining ranked as the second largest industry after agriculture in North Carolina. By the year 1840, North Carolina mines were producing gold worth over $1 million annually, thus making North Carolina the leading gold producer in America. North Carolina remained America's leading gold producer until 1848, when the California Gold Rush began and quickly overtook it in total production.There were changes in the mining operation that took place at Reed's estate over the following decades. At first, gold was extracted using the placer mining method from stream gravel. But soon enough, miners found out that gold could be found in veins of white quartz underground in the 1820s. Vein or lode mining was a much more costly operation than creek panning. Mining at Reed's mine began underground in 1831. Disputes in the family led to the mine's closure for ten years beginning in 1835, a closure that lasted until Reed died in 1845. His estate was sold in stages over the following decades. In 1895, it was purchased by Dr. Justin D. Lisle and the Kelly family for $15,000.The site of Reed’s discovery remains intact today as a North Carolina state historic site and a National Historic Landmark. The tunnels have been restored, and visitors can see exhibits tracing the mine's history, from the rock a boy carried home in 1799 to the discovery that followed.
Article Summary: Conrad Reed, a 12-year-old boy, found a 17-pound gold rock in Little Meadow Creek, North Carolina in 1799.
